characterList.description: A middle-aged man with short hair and glasses. He is wearing a dark blue jacket and a woolen beanie.
characterList.name: Narrator

content_metadata.description: A practical demonstration for optimizing a telescope setup to improve functionality, balance, and astrophotography results.

qAndA.answer: The narrator is using a fine adjustment mount, which allows for precise adjustments in altitude and azimuth.
qAndA.question: What type of mount is the narrator initially using for his finder scope?

qAndA.answer: The off-axis guider allows the narrator to achieve accurate tracking by finding multiple guide stars within the main telescope's field of view, eliminating the need for a separate guide scope.
qAndA.question: What is the advantage of using an off-axis guider?

qAndA.answer: The dew heater controller helps prevent condensation on the telescope lens by controlling the amount of power going to the dew heater strips.
qAndA.question: What is the purpose of the dew heater controller?

qAndA.answer: The narrator plans to increase the resistance of the resistors connected to the LEDs. This will reduce the current flowing through them, making them dimmer.
qAndA.question: How does the narrator plan to reduce the brightness of the LEDs on his control box?

qAndA.answer: The video focuses on demonstrating a practical approach to optimizing a telescope setup for astrophotography. It showcases techniques for weight reduction, cable management, and the use of an off-axis guider to achieve better balance and tracking accuracy.
qAndA.question: What is the overall narrative reasoning of the video?

activities.description: Narrator introduces a finder and mount.
Narrator points out the fine adjustment feature of the mount.
Narrator explains the combined weight of the finder and mount is 2 kg.

narrativeProgression.description: The narrator introduces the finder and mount, highlighting their features and combined weight.

scenes.title: Introduction of the Finder and Mount

activities.description: Narrator shows the imbalance in the telescope due to removing the finder and mount.
Narrator points out the solar scope and explains his plan to move electronics to balance the telescope.
Narrator explains how moving the electronics will reduce leverage on the mount.
Narrator mentions installing an off-axis guider.
Narrator explains the benefits of using the off-axis guider.

narrativeProgression.description: The narrator explains the problem caused by removing the finder and mount, his solution involving moving the electronics, and the successful implementation of an off-axis guider.

scenes.thematicElements: Astronomy equipment, weight balancing, problem-solving, astrophotography
scenes.title: Addressing Telescope Imbalance

activities.description: Narrator removes cables and electronics from the telescope tube.
Narrator talks about soldering cables to reduce their size and keep them tidy.

narrativeProgression.description: The narrator physically carries out his plan by removing and shortening cables to improve the setup's organization.

activities.description: Narrator shows a cable and explains his plan to shorten it.

narrativeProgression.description: The narrator focuses on a specific cable that needs shortening, further illustrating his attention to detail in optimizing the setup.

activities.description: Narrator shows a dew heater controller and explains its function.
Narrator points out the need to change resistors to reduce LED brightness.

narrativeProgression.description: The narrator introduces his homemade dew heater controller and addresses a minor issue with LED brightness, showcasing his DIY skills and problem-solving approach.

activities.description: Narrator shows an electronic control box with an Arduino and relay board.
Narrator explains the function of LEDs on the control box.
Narrator shows the inside of the control box, pointing out the Arduino, relay board, pins, ground, and resistors.
Narrator uses a multimeter to measure resistance and explains his plan to change resistor sizes.

narrativeProgression.description: The narrator dives deeper into the electronics, showing the components inside his control box and addressing the LED brightness issue with a plan to change resistor values.

activities.description: Narrator reconnects the electronic box to the telescope.
Narrator explains the components and their placement on the telescope.
Narrator sorts USB cables and fits the shortest ones possible.
Narrator shows all removed cables and weighs them.
Narrator weighs the finder, mount, and other removed components.

narrativeProgression.description: The narrator reassembles the setup with modified cables and components, showcasing the final result of his work and demonstrating the weight reduction achieved.

activities.description: Narrator thanks viewers for watching.
Narrator encourages viewers to like and subscribe.

narrativeProgression.description: The narrator concludes the video, expressing gratitude and encouraging viewer engagement.

climax.description: The narrator showcases the final, optimized setup and demonstrates the significant weight reduction achieved.

content_metadata.title: Telescope Setup Optimization

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: This is a quick observatory update. I've removed this finder and the mount.
The mount is one of those mounts that allows you to finally adjust it in altitude
and azimuth. It's a very nice mount but it's incredibly heavy. These two things
the mounts and the finder are two kilograms. So as a result my tube is no longer
balanced properly. I've got a solar scope down there as an William Optics ED80
and I had the other finder scope here balancing it out and now I've got more
weight on this side than I've got on this side. So my plan is to take all of
those cables and electronics that are currently opposite this bit here and
bring them to here and that'll help balance out the difference between the
weight of this and the weight of those bits. Those bits don't weigh anything
like as much as this but it will help a little and it'll reduce the leverage
that these things here are putting on the mount so it should make it easier
for the mount. I've been able to do this and remove the finder because I
installed an off-axis guide which has been brilliant. I get always multiple
stars to choose from. I'm using the latest version of PhD2 and with that you
can do multiple star alignment. On some occasions I'm getting eight stars that
it will find to do the tracking against. Which is pretty impressive given
it's an off-axis guide. It's quite a large chip. This is the QHY5 L2 mono.
Here I'm removing all of the cables and electronics from the telescope tube.
Now I've got all the cables off. I've got a few hours of soldering to reduce
the sizes of the cables so they're all nice and tidy. This cable only has to go
to there so I'm going to make it a lot shorter so it literally just goes to
there like that. This is what it looks like inside. This is my Juheater controller.
It's actually a Vellumon motor speed controller which does pulsed width modulation
to change the amount of power going to the output based on the resistance of
this potentiometer. This box is an Arduino and a four-channel relay control board.
It works with my as-concompliant power-buddy software. Since I've taken off the
telescope I thought I'd change the resistors in it because the LEDs that light up
have LEDs this side which is the input and then LEDs on this side which are the outputs.
They both light up when the relays are on but they're too bright so I need to
increase the resistor size on them to reduce the brightness of them.
This is what it looks like inside. Here's the Arduino, here's the four-channel relay board.
These are the pins that I'm using to control the relay board. There's four of them, one for each relay
and then there's also a ground which is getting off the Arduino and a power which
gets off the Arduino and then here is where you then wire up the relays to go from here.
Vider relay over to here and then these are the resistors that I need to change.
There's eight of them in total.
My electronics book says I need to use one kilone resistors for a 12 volt supply
and currently using 4.76 kilone and they're too bright so I'm probably going to look for
10 or 20 kilone's. Here I'm reconnecting the electronic boxes to the Vixen dovetail.
The electronics have plastic dovetail mount clamps which I've 3D printed and glued on.
The white box is my homemade Jew-heat controller. This is glued to my power buddy which is an
adscom compliant relay controller that I designed. The next two boxes from left to right are an
8 port USB 3 powered hub and a power distribution box. This takes the single 12 volt 30 amp supply
cable and splits it into five separate feeds. I do this to reduce the number of cables
traveling up the mount. I'll leave a link to my EQ6 cable management system in the description.
I measured how long each power cable needed to be and cut them down to size and resoldered the
connections. I then sorted through my USB cables and fitted the shortest cables possible.
A couple was still too long so I ordered shorter cables and fitted these off camera.
This is everything I've removed but the finder, the mount for the finder and then this is all of the
extra cable that I've cut out by moving where all the electronics is to a different position.
So that's all this cable. So the cable comes to 299 grams. I've taken into account the pot.
So I now reset the pot. We reset that to zero. We add on this. Got a thousand and 86 grams.
And then if we add this on, we've got 820 grams. So those three things together come to 2.2 kilograms.
I'm not sure that is in pounds, it's probably about five pounds. So that's quite a lot of weight
all removed by having an off axis guide. So I hope you've enjoyed this video. If you have please
click the thumbs up and if you'd like to see more videos like this then please click the subscribe

youtube_description:
Find out how I reduced the weight of my telescope by 5lb - perhaps you can too?
This is an update of my Telescope set-up following installation of an Off-axis-guider


In this video I'll take you through how and why I reduced the weight of my telescope by 5lb .

3:12 Power Buddy (I'll do a video on this in the new year)
